title: Consistent Distribution Matching for Data-Free Diffusion Distillation

paper.title: Consistent Distribution Matching for Data-Free Diffusion Distillation
paper.abstract: Abstract Flow and diffusion models suffer from slow inference due to computationally expensive numerical integration. Distillation provides a promising way for a student model to learn from a teacher’s dynamics, enabling one-step or few-step generation. However, existing methods often depend on curated distillation datasets, costly teacher rollouts, or auxiliary proxy networks, which complicate model training and scaling. In this work, we propose Consistent Distribution Matching, a simulation-free and data-free distillation method for accelerating diffusion and flow models while preserving strong generative capacity. Our key insight is to unify sample generation and score estimation with one student network. Thus, our framework uses only two models, a frozen teacher and a trainable student, and optimizes one objective. We prove that minimizing our objective indicates Wasserstein convergence of the student flow-map pushforwards to the teacher marginals. On ImageNet 256 × \times 256, our method attains an FID of 2.04 with a single function evaluation (1-NFE) and a 4-NFE FID of 1.37 within 40 epochs of training, surpassing the state-of-the-art distillation baselines without data. Our code code and model are available at https://consistentdmd.github.io/ .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion and flow-based generative models ( Albergo et al., 2023 ; Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ; Song et al., 2021 ; Karras et al., 2022 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Rombach et al., 2022 ; Tong et al., 2025 ) have become a leading framework for high-fidelity image and video synthesis. By learning a continuous transport from a simple prior distribution to a complex data distribution, these models provide stable training and strong sample quality across a wide spectrum of generative tasks ( Fu et al., 2025 ; Yan et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2023b ; Li et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Yan et al., 2025 ; Yin et al., 2025 ) . Despite these advantages, their inference cost remains non-trivial. The primary bottleneck lies in the iterative denoising procedure during inference. Generating a single sample requires numerically solving the differential equations governing the generative dynamics, which often involves hundreds of neural function evaluations. To address this challenge, diffusion distillation ( Geng et al., 2024 ; Song et al., 2023 ; Song and Dhariwal, 2023 ; Lu and Song, 2024 ; Meng et al., 2023 ; Frans et al., 2024 ; Sabour et al., 2025 ; Fu et al., 2025 ) provides a natural route to accelerate the generation with a new model. Given a powerful teacher diffuser, the student is trained to reproduce the teacher’s generative behavior while compressing the inference process in one or few steps. Existing distillation methods have made substantial progress, yet their training pipelines often introduce additional complexity. Some depend on heavy backward simulation ( Liu et al., 2023 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ; Gu et al., 2023 ) of a teacher diffusion model, auxiliary fake score networks ( Yin et al., 2024b ; Yin et al., 2024a ; Xie et al., 2024b ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2025d ; Luo et al., 2025 ; Ge et al., 2026 ) , adversarial objectives ( Zhou et al., 2025d ; Kim et al., 2023 ; Sauer et al., 2024 ; Sauer et al., 2025 ) , or multi-stage training ( Lee et al., 2024 ) . Although these components enable high-quality generation in few steps, they incur substantial memory overhead, impose an egregiously high optimization burden, and ultimately hinder the scalability of the distillation procedure. Figure 2: Curated 1024 × \times 1024 samples produced by our 4-step CDMD generator distilled from SANA1.6B LORA ( Xie et al., 2024a ) . Please zoom in for details. Beyond this procedural complexity, reliance on external distillation data ( Yin et al., 2024b ; Yin et al., 2024a ; Peng et al., 2025 ; Song et al., 2023 ; Lu and Song, 2024 ; Meng et al., 2023 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ) introduces a fundamental source of mismatch between data and teacher probability path. Data-based methods construct intermediate states by noising real data samples, often drawn from a distillation dataset that differs from the data used to train the teacher. Consequently, these states may deviate from those actually visited by the teacher during generation, causing the student to be supervised on a surrogate state distribution, instead of along the teacher’s probability path. This mismatch of the supervision states ( Tong et al., 2025 ) becomes pronounced when fine-tuning tilts the teacher’s distribution away from the original data ( Xie et al., 2024b ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) or when the teacher adopts classifier-free guidance ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) or autoguidance ( Karras et al., 2024 ) . In these settings, noising samples from the original data distribution provides progressively less faithful coverage of the states visited by the teacher. Moreover, when a teacher model is trained on proprietary data ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Wu et al., 2025 ; Seedream et al., 2025 ; Labs, 2025 ) , constructing such a data-anchored supervision path may be infeasible. Direct supervision on teacher trajectories would address the mismatch, but obtaining such states requires backward simulation, thereby reintroducing the aforementioned computational burden. This trade-off motivates our central question: can we distill a diffusion or flow teacher into a few-step student without external data, teacher rollouts, or auxiliary fake score models? We propose Consistent Distribution Matching Distillation (CDMD), a data-free and simulation-free framework for distilling diffusion and flow models using only a frozen teacher and a trainable student. Our framework aims to circumvent the distribution mismatch issues. Our central idea is to unify sample generation and score estimation within a single flow map model, eliminating the need for a separately trained proxy network. The student predicts average velocities over arbitrary denoising time intervals, supporting generation in one or a few steps. We bootstrap intermediate training states from student predictions and analytic forward noising, avoiding real data and teacher rollouts while allowing the training distribution to evolve with the student. Although these states do not necessarily coincide with those visited by the teacher during generation, our objective progressively aligns the corresponding student probability path with the teacher probability path. This enables the teacher to provide corrective velocity supervision directly on states relevant to the student’s generative dynamics. At these states, we regress the student velocity surrogate toward the teacher’s instantaneous velocity through a single objective. Moreover, as the states become noisier, they increasingly resemble the distributions encountered during teacher training, making the teacher’s velocity supervision more reliable. This trend is consistently observed across existing distribution matching baselines ( Yin et al., 2024a ; Yin et al., 2024b ) . The quality of the supervision also improves as the student distribution moves closers to the teacher distribution. We further establish a theoretical connection between local transport consistency and distribution matching. Under appropriate assumptions, minimizing population loss implies that the distributions induced by the student flow map converge to the teacher marginals in squared Wasserstein-2 distance averaged over time. Importantly, this result does not require the supervision states to be sampled from the teacher’s probability path. Next, the minimizer of our objective becomes the teacher average velocity. Overall, these results explain how local consistency can identify the teacher’s transport behavior and achieve distributional alignment without auxiliary score networks. Our contributions are threefold: 1. We introduce Consistent Distribution Matching Distillation, a data-free and simulation-free distillation framework for diffusion and flow-based generative models. The method uses only a frozen teacher and a trainable student, avoiding external distillation data, teacher rollouts and auxiliary proxy networks. 2. We provide a distribution-matching analysis showing that minimizing the proposed CDMD objective leads to narrowing the gap between the teacher distribution and the student distribution under regularity assumptions. The analysis also identifies the teacher’s average velocity field as the unique global minimizer for our objective. 3. We analyze the variance of the JVP correction in the data-free setting and validate the analysis on synthetic datasets. These results clarify when the correction improves stability and when student-teacher path mismatch can degrade training. On ImageNet256 × \times 256, Consistent Distribution Matching Distillation achieves a 1-NFE FID of 2.04 and a 4-NFE FID of 1.37 , achieving state-of-the-art performance among data-free distillation methods. In the text-to-image comparison when training data is inaccessible, our method leads most preference and alignment metrics and FID.

sections.heading: 3 Consistent Distribution Matching Distillation
sections.text: This section develops Consistent Distribution Matching Distillation as a distillation method without external data or teacher simulation, as illustrated in Fig. 3 . We first motivate supervision on states bootstrapped from the student model. Beyond the tradition KL divergence, we develop Consistent Distribution Matching from a Fisher-divergence criterion using a velocity surrogate derived from the student network. Finally, we relate the resulting consistency residual to distribution matching under regularity assumptions.

sections.heading: 5 Related work
sections.text: Trajectory Distillation. Distillation accelerates diffusion sampling by training students to reproduce the teacher’s dynamics in fewer steps. Knowledge distillation ( Zheng et al., 2023 ) learns a direct mapping from noise to data, while progressive distillation ( Salimans and Ho, 2022 ; Meng et al., 2023 ) repeatedly halves the number of sampling steps. Consistency models ( Lu and Song, 2024 ; Song and Dhariwal, 2023 ; Song et al., 2023 ; Luo et al., 2023a ) map states along the same ODE trajectory to a shared clean sample. Flow map distillation ( Boffi et al., 2025 ; Geng et al., 2025a ; Geng et al., 2025b ; Sabour et al., 2025 ; Lee et al., 2026 ) extends this idea to transitions between arbitrary times along a trajectory. BOOT ( Gu et al., 2023 ) , π \pi -Flow ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , and rectified flow ( Liu et al., 2023 ) explore ways to reduce reliance on real training data. For methods that require teacher reference trajectories, generating them during training or precomputing them can limit scalability as tasks become more complex. Our method avoids numerically integrating the teacher during training. Compared with FreeFlow ( Tong et al., 2025 ) , which anchors its flow map at noise, our model supports transitions from arbitrary input states and times.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented CDMD, a data-free and simulation-free framework for distilling pretrained diffusion and flow-based teachers into efficient one-step or few-step flow map students. Our method eliminates the need for external distillation data, teacher rollouts, backward simulation, and auxiliary proxy networks by training on a student-induced distribution with a single objective. Motivated by the velocity form Theoretically, we showed that, under regularity assumptions, minimizing our CDMD objective leads to convergence of student sampling distributions to teacher distributions in Wasserstein distance, averaged over reference times, and every global minimizer recovers the teacher average velocity on sampled states. Empirically, CDMD achieves state-of-the-art ImageNet256 × \times 256 generation quality among data-free distillation methods and further benefits from inference-time scaling through its parameterization. Our method also achieves the best overall performance in text-to-image generation, leading on both preference and alignment metrics as well as image-quality metrics. These results suggest that strong data-free distillation can be achieved with a simpler two-model training pipeline, while preserving the flexibility of multi-step sampling. Future work includes improving the stability of the JVP term, developing initialization strategies when no model weights are available, and extending the framework to large-scale generative tasks where data scarcity problem dominates.

sections.text: Tab. 4 compares representative distillation methods by the number of networks and optimizers they need, and by whether they require real data, trajectory simulation, or an adversarial objective. DMD2, SiD-LSG, SiDA, FreeFlow, and CTM train a third auxiliary network, either a fake-score model or a discriminator, with a second optimizer. BOOT is data-free but simulates trajectories during training. FACM and the flow map models (MF, CM, IMM) use only two networks and one optimizer, but they construct noisy states from real data. CDMD is the only method in the table that is both data-free and simulation-free while keeping only the teacher, the student, and a single optimizer. The subsections below relate CDMD to FreeFlow, flow maps, and DMD in more detail.

sections.heading: Architecture.
sections.text: Inspired by DMF ( Lee et al., 2026 ) , we investigate delaying endpoint conditioning to the later DiT blocks, as illustrated in Fig. 13 . It is important to note that our architecture also differs from DMF ( Lee et al., 2026 ) : rather than decoupling the t t and r r signals, we preserve the original time-conditioning branch throughout the network and inject the additional endpoint signal only into the later DiT blocks. We find this design to be more effective for data-free distillation. Empirically, we find that decoupling strategy from DMF can accelerate FID convergence during early training, but does not improve the final performance and can occasionally degrade it. We thereby ablate both the form of the conditioning signal and the layer at which endpoint-related information is introduced in the data-free setting. Our results show that conditioning on the interval t − r t-r , as in MeanFlow, consistently performs best. Moreover, for our 28-block student, injecting this signal from an intermediate block performs much better than injecting it in every block, with the best FID at block 8 8 under a 25K-iteration budget (Tab. 8 ); our full LightningDiT-XL/2 run uses block 10 10 (Tab. 5 ). Appendix E discusses this ablation in detail. Importantly, the original timestep t t remains available to all DiT blocks, while the additional t − r t-r conditioning is introduced only from block 10 10 onward. This design therefore differs from DMF: rather than fully decoupling the timestep and endpoint signals, we retain global conditioning on t t and selectively inject the interval signal into later layers.

sections.heading: D.3 Text-to-image Dataset
sections.text: To adapt our method on text-to-image dataset at a larger scale, some aspects need to be altered. First, we need to anchor on the teacher trajectory to prevent drifting effect. Similar to the baselines, we use 4 step during our inference. To control the noise added during training, we adopt the TDM ( Luo et al., 2025 ) method in our data-free setting. Every time we construct the intermediate states we start with the nearest earlier teacher checkpoint and we add noise according to the forward path. We decrease the variance of our target which leads to a better final performance. Fig. 10 illustrates this construction. The student generator first moves the prior sample backward along a coarse schedule, 𝒙 1 → 𝒙 ^ s → 𝒙 ^ r → 𝒙 ^ 0 {\bm{x}}_{1}\to\hat{{\bm{x}}}_{s}\to\hat{{\bm{x}}}_{r}\to\hat{{\bm{x}}}_{0} , and caches every intermediate state. A training state at time t t is then obtained by re-noising the nearest cached state that is cleaner than t t along the forward conditional path: 𝒙 ^ 0 \hat{{\bm{x}}}_{0} for t ∈ [ 0 , r ) t\in[0,r) , 𝒙 ^ r \hat{{\bm{x}}}_{r} for t ∈ [ r , s ) t\in[r,s) , and 𝒙 ^ s \hat{{\bm{x}}}_{s} for t ∈ [ s , 1 ] t\in[s,1] . Each re-noising step therefore covers a short interval, so the training states stay close to the 4-step trajectory used at inference. In this case, we observe more diversed background and better detailed being preserved from the teacher model. sections.heading: Appendix E Ablation on Endpoint Conditioning
sections.text: Fig. 13 compares how three transformer designs receive time information. (a) The DiT teacher predicts the instantaneous velocity and conditions every block on the embeddings of t t and the class label y y through adaLN-Zero. (b) The MeanFlow transformer predicts the average velocity and adds an embedding of the second time variable to the same signal, so every block sees both time variables. (c) The CDMD transformer keeps the teacher conditioning for the all blocks and adds the endpoint embedding, implemented as the gap t − r t-r , only to the last L − D L-D blocks and the final layer. Tab. 8 varies D D for the L = 28 L=28 student under a fixed budget of 25K iterations. At depth D D , the first D D blocks see only the teacher conditioning, and D = 0 D=0 conditions every block on ( t − r ) (t-r) , as in MeanFlow. Conditioning every block on the gap ( D = 0 D=0 ) gives an FID of 17.60, far worse than any delayed variant. Delaying the signal by five blocks already lowers FID to 2.80. All depths from 5 to 20 reach FID at most 2.80 and IS above 273, and D = 8 D=8 performs best with FID 2.21 and IS 284.46. Delaying the signal too far ( D = 25 D=25 ) raises FID to 3.84, since only three blocks remain to separate different intervals that start from the same ( 𝒙 t , t ) ({\bm{x}}_{t},t) . We interpret this effect through teacher capacity. The first D D blocks receive exactly the conditioning of the teacher, so they can reproduce the teacher features for the instantaneous velocity at ( 𝒙 t , t ) ({\bm{x}}_{t},t) , which every interval [ r , t ] [r,t] shares. The endpoint signal then only modulates the later blocks, which turn these shared features into the average velocity of a specific interval. With D = 0 D=0 , every block must handle both time variables from the start, and the student spends capacity on the endpoint before it reproduces the teacher. This matches our finding on the t t and r r schedule in Appendix F.2 : the conditioning depth and the fraction of t = r t=r pairs both control how much of the student stays dedicated to the teacher velocity, and preserving this teacher capacity is what keeps the distilled student close to the teacher.

sections.heading: F.1 Sampler Comparison with the SiT-XL/2+VA-REPA Teacher
sections.text: We further study inference-time scaling by comparing Euler, Heun, and DDIM samplers under different classifier-free guidance scales. Figure 11 reports FID as a function of the number of sampling steps for w = 1.5 w=1.5 and w = 2.0 w=2.0 . In some literatures ( Lee et al., 2026 ; Song et al., 2023 ) , DDIM method has also been referred as the Restart sampler. The ablation suggests that increasing the inference-time sampling budget does not automatically improve our distilled model. DDIM gives the strongest low-step performance in both guidance settings and remains especially stable from one to four steps. Euler is competitive at one or two steps for w = 1.5 w=1.5 , but its FID increases as more steps are used and then plateaus. Heun is the least stable in the low-step regime: it exhibits a sharp FID spike at two steps and only recovers after additional steps. The effect is more pronounced under stronger guidance, where both Euler and Heun drift to noticeably worse FID than DDIM as the sampling budget grows. These results give useful guidance for scaling inference time in our model. The interval-conditioned parameterization supports multi-step sampling, but the benefit depends strongly on the sampler and guidance scale. In this setting, DDIM is the most reliable choice for converting extra inference steps into stable sample quality, while higher-order or updates can amplify student-teacher mismatch at small step counts. We attribute this behavior primarily to these two factors. First, our training schedule assigns substantial probability mass to intervals with t ≠ r t\neq r , which may make the learned update less compatible with aggressive higher-order extrapolation at inference time. Second, the quality of the teacher, particularly its performance without CFG, has a pronounced effect on the distilled model. Empirically, we observe that differences in teacher performance without CFG translate into differences in the final student performance. Note that this student is trained with t = r t=r for only 10% of the pairs (Tab. 5 ). Appendix F.2 tests the first factor with a student trained with t = r t=r for 50% of the pairs.

sections.heading: F.2 Inference-time Scaling with the LightningDiT-XL/2 Teacher
sections.text: Fig. 12 repeats the inference-time scaling study for the student distilled from LightningDiT-XL/2. We sample the same student with Euler and DDIM from 1 to 64 steps without retraining. Unlike the SiT-XL/2+VA-REPA student in Fig. 11 , the Euler FID decreases from 2.04 at 1 step to 1.62 at 2 steps and 1.37 at 4 steps (Tab. 1 ), and reaches its minimum at 8 steps. From 8 to 64 steps, the Euler FID stays nearly flat and close to the teacher reference instead of drifting upward. The Euler IS rises from about 294 at 1 step to about 320 at 16 steps and then saturates. Additional steps thus refine the samples, as they do for the teacher FM model, and never cause the large degradation of the 10% t = r t=r student. The main difference between the two students is the training schedule. The LightningDiT student samples t = r t=r for 50% of the pairs, whereas the SiT-XL/2+VA-REPA student in Fig. 11 uses 10% (Tab. 5 ). On t = r t=r pairs, the objective reduces to ‖ 𝒖 𝜽 ​ ( 𝒙 ^ t , t , t ) − 𝒗 ⁡ ( 𝒙 ^ t , t ) ‖ 2 \norm{\vu_\vtheta(\hat{\vx}_t,t,t)-\vv(\hat{\vx}_t,t)}^{2} , so the student directly learns the teacher instantaneous velocity, which governs small sampling steps. DDIM behaves differently. Its FID is close to Euler at 1 and 2 steps but rises steadily after 4 steps and exceeds 5 at 64 steps, while its IS grows monotonically to above 420. Rising IS together with rising FID indicates that DDIM increasingly trades sample diversity for class fidelity as the number of steps grows. For this student, Euler is therefore the preferred sampler for inference-time scaling. sections.heading: Appendix G CDMD with Guidance
sections.text: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) is significant to class-conditional image generation because it facilitates conditional generation by extrapolating from unconditional to conditional predictions. Since the most pre-trained diffusion baselines are evaluated with CFG, we formulate our distillation objective to match the guided teacher dynamics rather than the unguided velocity field alone. Let 𝒗 ⁡ ( 𝒙 t , t ∣ 𝒄 ) {\bm{v}}({\bm{x}}_{t},t\mid{\bm{c}}) and 𝒗 ⁡ ( 𝒙 t , t ∣ ∅ ) {\bm{v}}({\bm{x}}_{t},t\mid\varnothing) denote the conditional and unconditional teacher velocity fields, respectively. For a guidance scale w ≥ 1 w\geq 1 , the guided velocity field is defined as 𝒗 cfg ​ ( 𝒙 t , t ∣ 𝒄 ) = ( 1 − w ) ​ 𝒗 ​ ( 𝒙 t , t ∣ ∅ ) + w ​ 𝒗 ​ ( 𝒙 t , t ∣ 𝒄 ) . {\bm{v}}^{\text{cfg}}({\bm{x}}_{t},t\mid{\bm{c}})=(1-w)\,{\bm{v}}({\bm{x}}_{t},t\mid\varnothing)+w\,{\bm{v}}({\bm{x}}_{t},t\mid{\bm{c}}). In addition, we can reinforce this signal by incorporating student guidance with scale α ≥ 0 \alpha\geq 0 during training to support 1-NFE sampling ( Geng et al., 2025a ) . Compared with standard CFG sampling, which evaluates both conditional and unconditional branches at each solver step and therefore doubles the NFE count, this training-time guided target lets the distilled student absorb part of the conditional guidance signal before inference. Specifically, we define the enhanced guided velocity field as follows: 𝒗 cfg++ ​ ( 𝒙 t , t ∣ 𝒄 ) = 𝒗 cfg ​ ( 𝒙 t , t ∣ 𝒄 ) + α ⁡ ( 𝒖 𝜽 ​ ( 𝒙 t , t , t ∣ 𝒄 ) − 𝒖 𝜽 ​ ( 𝒙 t , t , t ∣ ∅ ) ) , {\bm{v}}^{\text{cfg++}}({\bm{x}}_{t},t\mid{\bm{c}})={\bm{v}}^{\text{cfg}}({\bm{x}}_{t},t\mid{\bm{c}})+\alpha\Big({\bm{u}}_{\bm{\theta}}({\bm{x}}_{t},t,t\mid{\bm{c}})-{\bm{u}}_{\bm{\theta}}({\bm{x}}_{t},t,t\mid\varnothing)\Big), (37) where 𝒖 𝜽 ​ ( 𝒙 t , t , t ∣ 𝒄 ) {\bm{u}}_{\bm{\theta}}({\bm{x}}_{t},t,t\mid{\bm{c}}) approximates the ground-truth instantaneous marginal velocity field under condition 𝒄 {\bm{c}} . This additional term further amplifies the conditional signal while retaining the stabilizing effect of the unconditional component. Following the flexible guidance in iMF ( Geng et al., 2025b ) , we allow the network to condition on the guidance term.

Fig. 14 shows that the best w w depends on both the teacher checkpoint and the EMA rate. Moderate w w gives the best FID in most settings, while large w w or strong EMA smoothing degrades it. For the SiT-XL/2+VA-REPA teacher, all three EMA settings reach their lowest FID at w ∈ [ 1.8 , 1.9 ] w\in[1.8,1.9] . The student without EMA attains the lowest FID-50K of about 2.93, whereas an EMA decay of 0.9999 raises the minimum to about 3.38. For the SiT-XL/2 teacher, the optimum shifts to w ≈ 2.0 w\approx 2.0 , and the student without EMA again performs best at about 3.47. We also observe that student guidance is difficult to tune with Lightning-DiT as the teacher, so we set α = 0 \alpha=0 . It occasionally yields a very high IS with exaggerated class features.

sections.heading: Appendix H Limitations and broader impact
sections.text: A key limitation of the current formulation is the absence of meaningful constraints on the total derivative term d d t ⁡ 𝒖 ⁡ ( 𝒙 t , t , r ) = 𝒗 ⁡ ( 𝒙 t , t ) ​ D 𝒙 t ​ 𝒖 + ∂ t 𝒖 \derivative{t}{\bm{u}}({\bm{x}}_{t},t,r)={\bm{v}}({\bm{x}}_{t},t)D_{{\bm{x}}_{t}}{\bm{u}}+\partial_{t}{\bm{u}} . To date, this component has not been rigorously analyzed. In prior work, it is typically detached from the computational graph and excluded from backpropagation, effectively treating it as a constant. However, empirical observations reveal that its norm is large and fluctuates substantially throughout training, suggesting that this simplification may be problematic. A plausible direction for regularization is to leverage a well-trained reference velocity field 𝒗 ⁡ ( 𝒙 t , t ) {\bm{v}}({\bm{x}}_{t},t) , encouraging the derivative term to exhibit similar, more stable behavior. In practice, not only is the dataset private, but the teacher model weights are also inaccessible. Hence, we cannot initialize the student model with the teacher model weights, which is a common practice in distillation work. This makes training more challenging and less stable. Moreover, we speculate that for different tasks, the way we bootstrapped our x t x_{t} is of great importance. This can substantially influence the learning dynamics and overall effectiveness of distillation.

Distillation provides a promising way for a student model to learn from a teacher’s dynamics, enabling one-step or few-step generation. However, existing methods often depend on curated distillation datasets, costly teacher rollouts, or auxiliary proxy networks, which complicate model training and scaling. In this work, we propose Consistent Distribution Matching, a simulation-free and data-free distillation method for accelerating diffusion and flow models while preserving strong generative capacity. Our key insight is to unify sample generation and score estimation with one student network. Thus, our framework uses only two models, a frozen teacher and a trainable student, and optimizes one objective. We prove that minimizing our objective indicates Wasserstein convergence of the student flow-map pushforwards to the teacher marginals. On ImageNet 256 × 	imes 256, our method attains an FID of 2.04 with a single function evaluation (1-NFE) and a 4-NFE FID of 1.37 within 40 epochs of training, surpassing the state-of-the-art distillation baselines without data. Our method aligns the marginal probability paths of the teacher p t p_{t} and the student q t q_{t} without requiring curated distillation data or computationally intensive simulations. 1 Introduction Diffusion and flow-based generative models ( Albergo et al., 2023 ; Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ; Song et al., 2021 ; Karras et al., 2022 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Rombach et al., 2022 ; Tong et al., 2025 ) have become a leading framework for high-fidelity image and video synthesis. By learning a continuous transport from a simple prior distribution to a complex data distribution, these models provide stable training and strong sample quality across a wide spectrum of generative tasks ( Fu et al., 2025 ; Yan et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2023b ; Li et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Yan et al., 2025 ; Yin et al., 2025 ) . Despite these advantages, their inference cost remains non-trivial. The primary bottleneck lies in the iterative denoising procedure during inference. Generating a single sample requires numerically solving the differential equations governing the generative dynamics, which often involves hundreds of neural function evaluations. To address this challenge, diffusion distillation ( Geng et al., 2024 ; Song et al., 2023 ; Song and Dhariwal, 2023 ; Lu and Song, 2024 ; Meng et al., 2023 ; Frans et al., 2024 ; Sabour et al., 2025 ; Fu et al., 2025 ) provides a natural route to accelerate the generation with a new model. Given a powerful teacher diffuser, the student is trained to reproduce the teacher’s generative behavior while compressing the inference process in one or few steps. Existing distillation methods have made substantial progress, yet their training pipelines often introduce additional complexity. Some depend on heavy backward simulation ( Liu et al., 2023 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ; Gu et al., 2023 ) of a teacher diffusion model, auxiliary fake score networks ( Yin et al., 2024b ; Yin et al., 2024a ; Xie et al., 2024b ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2025d ; Luo et al., 2025 ; Ge et al., 2026 ) , adversarial objectives ( Zhou et al., 2025d ; Kim et al., 2023 ; Sauer et al., 2024 ; Sauer et al., 2025 ) , or multi-stage training ( Lee et al., 2024 ) . Although these components enable high-quality generation in few steps, they incur substantial memory overhead, impose an egregiously high optimization burden, and ultimately hinder the scalability of the distillation procedure. Figure 2: Curated 1024 × 	imes 1024 samples produced by our 4-step CDMD generator distilled from SANA1.6B LORA ( Xie et al., 2024a ) . Please zoom in for details. Beyond this procedural complexity, reliance on external distillation data ( Yin et al., 2024b ; Yin et al., 2024a ; Peng et al., 2025 ; Song et al., 2023 ; Lu and Song, 2024 ; Meng et al., 2023 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ) introduces a fundamental source of mismatch between data and teacher probability path. Data-based methods construct intermediate states by noising real data samples, often drawn from a distillation dataset that differs from the data used to train the teacher. Consequently, these states may deviate from those actually visited by the teacher during generation, causing the student to be supervised on a surrogate state distribution, instead of along the teacher’s probability path. This mismatch of the supervision states ( Tong et al., 2025 ) becomes pronounced when fine-tuning tilts the teacher’s distribution away from the original data ( Xie et al., 2024b ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) or when the teacher adopts classifier-free guidance ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) or autoguidance ( Karras et al., 2024 ) . In these settings, noising samples from the original data distribution provides progressively less faithful coverage of the states visited by the teacher. Moreover, when a teacher model is trained on proprietary data ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Wu et al., 2025 ; Seedream et al., 2025 ; Labs, 2025 ) , constructing such a data-anchored supervision path may be infeasible. Direct supervision on teacher trajectories would address the mismatch, but obtaining such states requires backward simulation, thereby reintroducing the aforementioned computational burden. This trade-off motivates our central question: can we distill a diffusion or flow teacher into a few-step student without external data, teacher rollouts, or auxiliary fake score models? We propose Consistent Distribution Matching Distillation (CDMD), a data-free and simulation-free framework for distilling diffusion and flow models using only a frozen teacher and a trainable student. Our framework aims to circumvent the distribution mismatch issues. Our central idea is to unify sample generation and score estimation within a single flow map model, eliminating the need for a separately trained proxy network. The student predicts average velocities over arbitrary denoising time intervals, supporting generation in one or a few steps. We bootstrap intermediate training states from student predictions and analytic forward noising, avoiding real data and teacher rollouts while allowing the training distribution to evolve with the student. Although these states do not necessarily coincide with those visited by the teacher during generation, our objective progressively aligns the corresponding student probability path with the teacher probability path. This enables the teacher to provide corrective velocity supervision directly on states relevant to the student’s generative dynamics. At these states, we regress the student velocity surrogate toward the teacher’s instantaneous velocity through a single objective. Moreover, as the states become noisier, they increasingly resemble the distributions encountered during teacher training, making the teacher’s velocity supervision more reliable. This trend is consistently observed across existing distribution matching baselines ( Yin et al., 2024a ; Yin et al., 2024b ) . The quality of the supervision also improves as the student distribution moves closers to the teacher distribution. We further establish a theoretical connection between local transport consistency and distribution matching. Under appropriate assumptions, minimizing population loss implies that the distributions induced by the student flow map converge to the teacher marginals in squared Wasserstein-2 distance averaged over time. Importantly, this result does not require the supervision states to be sampled from the teacher’s probability path. Next, the minimizer of our objective becomes the teacher average velocity. Overall, these results explain how local consistency can identify the teacher’s transport behavior and achieve distributional alignment without auxiliary score networks. Our contributions are threefold: 1. We introduce Consistent Distribution Matching Distillation, a data-free and simulation-free distillation framework for diffusion and flow-based generative models. The method uses only a frozen teacher and a trainable student, avoiding external distillation data, teacher rollouts and auxiliary proxy networks. 2. We provide a distribution-matching analysis showing that minimizing the proposed CDMD objective leads to narrowing the gap between the teacher distribution and the student distribution under regularity assumptions. The analysis also identifies the teacher’s average velocity field as the unique global minimizer for our objective. 3. We analyze the variance of the JVP correction in the data-free setting and validate the analysis on synthetic datasets. These results clarify when the correction improves stability and when student-teacher path mismatch can degrade training. On ImageNet256 × 	imes 256, Consistent Distribution Matching Distillation achieves a 1-NFE FID of 2.04 and a 4-NFE FID of 1.37 , achieving state-of-the-art performance among data-free distillation methods.
